intro: An egg goes from clear to white in a hot pan. A batter stirred a minute too long bakes into a tough, peaked muffin. A sauce stays thin for ten minutes and then thickens all at once. A dressing shaken hard looks creamy and then, an hour later, splits back into oil and vinegar. None of this is luck, and none of it is mystery. Each one is a chemical or physical change that a cook can see, predict and control. This unit opens the lid on what is really happening inside food when heat, stirring, acid, fat or time gets to it.

The first chapter follows the big three of baking and cooking. Proteins unfold and set. Starches swell and thicken. Wheat flour builds a gluten web when it is wetted and worked. Along the way you will learn how baking soda, baking powder, yeast and steam each lift a dough. You will see why a dry hot surface browns and a wet one steams. You will find out what acids and bases do to color, texture and flavor. Every lesson starts at the stove or the mixing bowl, with real amounts and real temperatures. Each ends with the rule that explains what you saw.

The second chapter turns the kitchen into a laboratory. You will build a vinaigrette by ratio and a mayonnaise drop by drop. You will learn why an emulsion breaks and how to fix it. You will find out what fat and sugar do in a recipe beyond taste. Then you will run a real experiment, one variable at a time, with a control, a data table and an honest write-up. The unit closes with the science of keeping food: freezing at 0 °F, drying, and canning. There, knowing the difference between a high-acid and a low-acid food is the difference between a safe pantry and a dangerous one. By the end you will be able to look at any recipe and say not only what to do but why it works.
bigQuestion: What is really happening inside food when a cook applies heat, mixing, acid, fat or time, and how can you test it for yourself?

timeline.t: Egyptian bakers leave dough to rise with wild yeast, the first leavened bread
Cooks in many cultures preserve food by salting, drying and fermenting long before anyone knows why it works
Nicolas Appert publishes his method of sealing food in glass jars and heating them, the start of canning
John Dwight and Austin Church begin making baking soda in New York, putting a chemical leavener in American kitchens
John L. Mason patents the threaded glass jar with a screw-on lid used for home canning ever since
Louis Pasteur shows that heating a liquid kills the microbes that spoil it, the basis of pasteurization
Fannie Farmer's Boston Cooking-School Cook Book insists on level, exact measurements
Kikunae Ikeda identifies glutamate as the source of the savory taste he names umami
Louis-Camille Maillard describes the browning reaction between amino acids and sugars
Clarence Birdseye develops quick-freezing, making frozen food a practical way to keep quality
Harold McGee's On Food and Cooking brings kitchen chemistry to home cooks and chefs
USDA-tested canning recipes and safe temperatures are the standard every home cook follows

test.q: What links unfolded egg proteins into a solid as an egg cooks?
test.why: After heat denatures the proteins, coagulation bonds them into a net that turns the liquid egg solid.

test.q: A muffin batter should be stirred how much?
choices: For three minutes on a mixer
Just until the dry flour disappears, lumps and all
test.why: Extra stirring builds gluten, which makes tough, peaked, tunneled muffins.

test.q: Why does a roux keep a sauce from getting lumpy?
choices: The fat coats each starch grain before the liquid arrives
The butter makes the milk hotter
The flour is cooked into sugar
test.why: Starch grains coated in fat cannot clump and seal over when they meet hot liquid.

test.q: Which ingredient must a recipe contain for baking soda to lift it?
choices: An acid such as buttermilk, yogurt or lemon juice
test.why: Soda is a base; it releases carbon dioxide only when an acid and liquid are present.

test.q: What is the proofing range for active dry yeast in water?
test.why: Yeast wakes and foams in water at about 105 to 115 °F; above about 140 °F it dies.

test.q: Two trays of chicken thighs: one spaced out, one crowded. Why does the crowded tray stay pale?
choices: The oven cannot heat a full tray
Crowded pieces cook faster and are removed too soon
Moisture from the crowd holds the surface near 212 °F, too cool for browning
test.why: The Maillard reaction needs a dry surface well above boiling; a crowded pan steams.

test.q: On the pH scale, lemon juice at about 2 is which of the following?
test.why: Numbers below 7 are acidic; lemon juice near 2 is strongly acidic.

test.q: What is the standard ratio of oil to acid in a vinaigrette?
test.why: Three parts oil to one part vinegar or lemon juice is the base ratio, scaled up or down as needed.

test.q: Mayonnaise turns thin and greasy while it is being made. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The lemon juice was added first
Oil added too fast for the yolk's lecithin to coat the droplets
The bowl was made of glass
test.why: An emulsion breaks when oil arrives faster than the emulsifier can coat it and the droplets merge.

test.q: Why can oil brown food when water cannot?
choices: Oil can be heated far above 212 °F, the limit of water in an open pan
test.why: Browning needs surface temperatures well above boiling, which oil reaches and water never does.

test.q: Cold butter is cut into flour in pea-sized pieces for a pie crust. What does that produce in the oven?
choices: Flaky layers as the pieces melt and steam apart
A crust that does not brown
test.why: Separate cold fat pieces leave gaps and their water becomes steam, lifting the layers apart.

test.q: A student cuts a cake's sugar in half and the cake is pale, dry and tough. Which of sugar's jobs explains the toughness?
choices: Sugar competes with flour proteins for water, limiting gluten
test.why: Less sugar leaves more water for the flour proteins, so more gluten forms and the crumb toughens.

test.q: In a fair experiment on cookie spread, what should be true of the control batch?
choices: It is the batch with the most changes
It is made exactly by the original recipe with nothing changed
test.why: The control gives the baseline every changed batch is compared against.

choices: Under cold running water in a sealed bag
In the microwave, then cooking right away
On the counter through the afternoon
test.why: Counter thawing leaves the surface in the 40 to 140 °F danger zone for hours.

test.q: Why must green beans be canned in a pressure canner rather than a boiling-water bath?
choices: They are a low-acid food, and only pressure-canner heat kills botulism spores
They are too hard to soften in boiling water
Beans need less time than fruit
test.why: Low-acid foods cannot stop Clostridium botulinum; killing its spores needs the above-boiling heat of a pressure canner.

write.prompt: Design a kitchen experiment that tests one change to a recipe you know, such as chilling the dough, swapping the sugar or changing the fat. Write the question, the hypothesis, the full method with exact amounts and every constant, the data table you will fill, and the safety steps for the food involved. Then explain why each part of the plan is there.
tips: Change exactly one variable and name it; everything else stays constant.
Include a control batch made by the original recipe.
Say what you will measure, with what tool, and how many trials you will average.
Name the safety rule for the food: safe temperatures, the two-hour rule, or safe thawing.
Check the numbers: amounts, oven temperature and times must match across every batch.
